entries.title: [Editorial] Transforming the humanitarian system
entries.description: We are witnessing a dark period for humanity. Recent years have been the most violent since the Cold War. Conflict-related deaths hit a 20-year high in 2022, while more than 123 million people have been forcibly displaced. Sudan, Gaza, and Ukraine lay bare the realities of modern conflict. Violation of international law and humanitarian principles has been normalised. Health-care workers and facilities as well as civilian infrastructure are targeted with impunity. Aid is instrumentalised for military ends and increasingly becomes transactional.

entries.title: [Comment] Transforming the humanitarian system: our role to confront embedded inequities
entries.description: The humanitarian system presents itself as a beacon of hope amid humanitarian crises, a vision that drew many of us into the field of humanitarian work. Yet once inside, the ideal unravels. Rooted in colonial histories and perpetuated by enduring global power asymmetries and the neoliberal logic of the aid sector, the humanitarian system frequently reinforces the very inequities it purports to resolve.1 These inequities manifest through policies and frameworks, as well as via interpersonal and cultural practices that, implicitly or explicitly, marginalise the most vulnerable.

entries.title: [Comment] Astegolimab and the new era of biologics in COPD care
entries.description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) affects 480 million people worldwide and this is projected to increase to nearly 600 million over the next two decades.1 Long-acting beta agonists (LABA) and long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA), often combined with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS), are the cornerstone of COPD management.2 However, even with maximal inhaled therapy, most patients remain symptomatic and a third continue to have multiple exacerbations.3

entries.title: [Comment] Measuring mental disorder burden for action
entries.description: Quantifying the burden of mental disorders is essential, yet inherently reductive. Metrics such as disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and years lived with disability (YLDs) provide a highly important common framework for comparing diseases across settings, but they only partly reflect lived experience. Such figures cannot fully capture the distress of a father whose daughter experiences persistent suicidal thoughts, or the impact on the quality of life of a child whose mother is unable to leave the house due to paranoid ideas.

entries.title: [Comment] Offline: The future of war
entries.description: Every week I have a 1-h call with a friend who lives on the US west coast, among tech entrepreneurs and fledgling billionaires. He is not a member of that tribe, but he does stalk their hinterland. Occasionally, he is invited to their top table, to contribute his own particular brand of esoteric wisdom, but more interestingly to eavesdrop on their thoughts and preoccupations. Perhaps because of where he lives, he leans towards techno-optimism. But sometimes optimism can trigger apocalyptic reflection.

entries.title: [Perspectives] Justice out of time: infected blood and patient knowledge
entries.description: Questions over right and wrong in past medical practices all too frequently resist easy answers. Formal ethical frameworks, and the imperfect ways that they are interpreted and applied, are products of their time; and so are reflections on the past from the shifting and incomplete vantage point of the present. Historical injustices, such as the use of psychosurgery for behavioural and mental health problems during the mid-20th century, stretch understandings of what kinds of judgement are possible when a significant degree of time has elapsed.

entries.description: The Thalassaemia International Federation is issuing a belated, albeit necessary and desperate, plea on behalf of patients with thalassaemia who are direct witnesses and, increasingly, victims of armed conflict. Even sanctions, used as a non-military foreign policy tool and to gain the political upper hand, constitute a battlefield for these susceptible populations.

entries.title: [Correspondence] Loans, leases, and labour: the cost of becoming a doctor in the UK
entries.description: 6 years ago, I questioned whether a medical career was financially realistic given my financial background and the funding options available to students. Now, as a fifth-year medical student at University College London (London, UK), that concern highlights a broader structural issue within UK medical education funding. In England, most medical students receive full tuition and maintenance support for the first 4 years. For those on 6-year programmes, the final 2 years are funded by a reduced maintenance loan, alongside a National Health Service bursary and variable supplementary support.

entries.title: [Comment] A much-needed reboot for international solidarity
entries.description: In my 40 years as a humanitarian worker, I have never seen such a gap between documented acute need for medical and other humanitarian assistance, and global solidarity to meet those needs. In decades of humanitarian crises, this gap has never been so vast.1 To be blunt: tens of millions of people are today left on their own, meeting their hour of deepest need with nowhere to turn. Millions of people do not have real international or local assistance, and receive only what their communities and extended families can muster between themselves.

entries.title: [Comment] Making mutual aid the architecture of humanitarian response
entries.description: The humanitarian system is not failing for lack of diagnosis. For a decade, commissions, reviews, and reform frameworks have identified the same structural pathology: resources, authority, and legitimacy are concentrated in international institutions that are systematically less effective, less accountable, and less trusted than the communities they claim to serve. The Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health–Lancet Commission on health, conflict, and forced displacement1 adds rigour and normative weight to this diagnosis.

entries.title: [Perspectives] Paul B Spiegel: pioneer in humanitarian health
entries.description: Paul B Spiegel is widely regarded as exceptional among high-ranking academics. As his Co-Chair on the Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health–Lancet Commission on Health, Conflict, and Forced Displacement, Karl Blanchet says Spiegel is “a rare professor: one foot in the field, one foot in the university”. The field of humanitarian health has long been Spiegel's passion. As a teenager, he read a TIME magazine article about Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), which inspired him to go to medical school.

entries.title: Will Robotics Have a ChatGPT Moment?
